name: starter
title: MetaRush starter pack
about: The starter abilities from MetaRush's own repository: stock and openly licensed media, sound effects, English captions, pictures from a ComfyUI server on your computer.

abilities.name: comfyui-local
abilities.title: Pictures from ComfyUI on this computer
abilities.does: Makes pictures from a few words with the ComfyUI server running on this computer, using a model you already have in it.
abilities.notes:
# Pictures from ComfyUI on this computer

Sends a text-to-picture graph (a checkpoint, your words and the words to avoid, a size, steps and a seed) to the
ComfyUI server running on this computer, waits for it, and brings the pictures back. Bring your own GPU and your own
models: nothing is downloaded and nothing leaves this computer.

- **ComfyUI is GPL-3.0 software you install and run yourself, beside MetaRush.** Nothing of it is bundled with
  MetaRush or in this folder; this ability only talks to it over HTTP. Install it from its own project (the ComfyUI
  desktop app, or `git clone` and its `requirements.txt` in a Python environment of yours), put a checkpoint in its
  `models/checkpoints` folder and start it on 127.0.0.1, port 8188 (its default).
- **The one thing on this computer it reaches**: an owner agrees, when approving it, that it may reach
  ComfyUI on port 8188 of the computer it runs on (`metarush ability approve comfyui-local --local-service`, or the
  approval question in Library → Abilities), after seeing the program listening there: Python's executable, the
  folder ComfyUI was started in and the script it runs (`main.py`), and that it answers `/system_stats` as ComfyUI
  does. Only that program is reached: plans show it, each run checks it as it starts and while it runs, and another
  program on the port — a plain `python3 -m http.server`, say — is refused. Moved or restarted from another folder,
  ComfyUI needs an owner to agree again (`metarush ability setup comfyui-local --agree-local` on that computer). The
  run's proxy then forwards plain HTTP to 127.0.0.1:8188 and records each request; every other port of this computer, every local network and the internet stay closed. ComfyUI itself
  runs outside MetaRush's sandbox with your rights, so whatever it can do (custom nodes included), a run may ask it
  to: that is why a person starts each run, and why only an owner agrees to it.
- **Another port:** a ComfyUI on another port needs a version of this ability whose `local` says that port, and an
  owner's approval of that version; the script reads the address MetaRush gives it (`$METARUSH_LOCAL_URL`), so only
  the manifest's line changes.
- **Licence of the pictures:** whatever your checkpoint's licence says; the pictures are AI-generated, so say so
  where you publish them. (MetaRush doesn't yet mark pictures an ability made as AI-generated in deliveries; AI services
 do, for the work they make.)
- **Licence of this ability's code:** MIT.
- **Cost:** free; your computer does the work.
- **Key:** none.
- **What leaves this computer:** nothing through MetaRush. Your words go to ComfyUI on this computer, which runs
  outside the sandbox: if you added nodes that reach the internet (API nodes, a model manager), they may send things
  on by themselves.
- **Who starts a run:** a person, each time.

What it doesn't do yet: pictures as input (image to image) and ComfyUI's WebSocket progress; a run waits up to 25
minutes, checking every second.

abilities.name: english-captions
abilities.title: English captions by whisper.cpp
abilities.does: Writes English captions for a clip spoken in another language, translated on this computer by whisper.cpp, and keeps them with the clip.
abilities.notes:
# English captions by whisper.cpp

Translates the speech of a clip in another language into English captions on this computer, and keeps them with
the clip: `metarush footage captions <clip> --language en` shows them (`--save english.srt` writes the file). It
wraps what MetaRush already uses: ffmpeg turns the clip's sound into 16 kHz mono, and whisper.cpp's `whisper-cli`
translates it (`-tr`) into SRT captions. The captions are marked as machine-translated.

They are the clip's, beside its transcript: a cut's own captions, and the translations Claude writes for them line
by line (`captions translate`), don't change. Use them to read what a clip says, as a reference for a translation,
or as a captions file for the clip itself.

- **What it needs on each computer** (a person sets it up):
  `metarush ability setup english-captions --file whisper-model=/full/path/ggml-medium.bin`
  - `ffmpeg` and `whisper-cli` (whisper.cpp; Homebrew: `brew install ffmpeg whisper-cpp`), pinned by fingerprint.
  - A whisper.cpp model **that can translate**: `ggml-medium.bin` (1.5 GB, a good balance), `ggml-small.bin`
    (faster, rougher) or `ggml-large-v3.bin` (3 GB, best). The turbo model MetaRush uses to write words down
    (`ggml-large-v3-turbo.bin`) was not trained to translate and only writes the language it hears; English-only
    models (`*.en.bin`) can't either. Download one from the whisper.cpp project's models (its
    `models/download-ggml-model.sh medium`) anywhere you like, then set it up as above. MetaRush pins it by its
    fingerprint and copies it into each run, read-only (an APFS clone on a Mac, so no extra space); the ability
    never reads it in place.
- **Licences:** whisper.cpp is MIT; OpenAI's Whisper models are MIT. This ability's code is MIT.
- **Cost:** free; it runs on this computer, **on the CPU**: MetaRush's sandbox doesn't open the GPU to abilities
  (whisper.cpp's Metal start-up is refused there), so it runs whisper-cli with `-ng`. That is slower than MetaRush's
  own transcription: on a recent Mac, expect around a minute per minute of speech with `ggml-small.bin` and several
  with `ggml-medium.bin` or `ggml-large-v3.bin`; a run may take up to an hour.
- **Key:** none.
- **What leaves this computer:** nothing; its network is off.
- **Who starts a run:** anyone, and Claude as a safe step: it is free, local and sends nothing.

Say the language (`language: es`) when you know it; otherwise whisper.cpp listens first. Captions come one
sentence at a time, as whisper.cpp hears them.

abilities.name: freesound-effects
abilities.title: Sound effects from Freesound
abilities.does: Finds sound effects on Freesound that match a few words and brings them in, each with its licence and the credit it asks for. Freesound's API is free for non-commercial use only.
abilities.notes:
# Sound effects from Freesound

Searches Freesound for a few words and brings in up to six sounds no longer than you say (30 seconds unless you
change it), as Freesound's high-quality previews (MP3, about 128 kbps). Each sound keeps its licence, its page, who
recorded it and the credit line its licence asks for, e.g. “Rain on a tin roof” by rain_maker, CC BY 4.0, via
Freesound; it records them as its rights, and a delivery lists them with its credits and in its `.notes.md` file.

- **Licences of the sounds:** CC0 (no credit needed) and CC BY (credit needed) by default, or CC0 only. Sounds under
  "non-commercial" (CC BY-NC) or Sampling+ are left out, and the run's log says so.
- **Freesound's API terms:** using the API is free **only for non-commercial purposes**; for commercial work
  Freesound asks you to contact them first. That is about the API, not the sounds' licences: check it before using
  this ability for a client.
- **Licence of this ability's code:** MIT.
- **Cost:** free. Freesound allows 60 requests a minute and 2,000 a day per key.
- **Key:** `freesound`, free with a Freesound account (freesound.org/apiv2/apply). An owner adds it on each computer:
  `metarush ability setup freesound-effects --key freesound`. The code never sees it: MetaRush puts it in the
  Authorization header (as `Token <key>`), only on requests to freesound.org.
- **What leaves this computer:** the words you search for, to freesound.org. The previews come from
  cdn.freesound.org without the key.
- **Who starts a run:** a person, each time (it uses a key).

What's missing: the original files (WAV, FLAC at full quality) need a Freesound sign-in through OAuth2, which
abilities can't do; MetaRush keeps keys, not sign-ins. Previews are enough for most effects under a voice.

Search with the thing and the action: "door creak", "rain on roof", "crowd cheering", "whoosh".

abilities.name: open-media
abilities.title: Public-domain and openly licensed media
abilities.does: Finds public-domain and openly licensed pictures, video and sound on Wikimedia Commons and the Internet Archive and brings them in, each with its licence and the credit it asks for.
abilities.notes:
# Public-domain and openly licensed media

Searches Wikimedia Commons and the Internet Archive (or one of them) and brings in up to six pictures, videos or
sounds, taking turns between the two. Only files you may use and change in any video come in: public domain (and
the Public Domain Mark), CC0, CC BY and CC BY-SA. Anything non-commercial (NC), "no derivatives" (ND), fair use,
unclear or unstated is left out, and the run's log says why.

Each file keeps its licence, its page, its author and the credit line its licence asks for — title, author,
licence and where it came from, e.g. “Harbour light” by Sea Painter, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. A clip or
sound records them as its rights; a picture on its source. Delivering a video that uses them lists the credits in
the delivery's record and writes them into the `.notes.md` file next to the video, ready to paste into a
description. CC BY-SA asks that what you make from the file is shared under the same licence: check before using
one in a client's video.

- **Licence of the files:** per file, as above. Wikimedia sometimes adds restrictions (trademarks, a person's
  likeness); the run's log names them.
- **Licence of this ability's code:** MIT.
- **Cost:** free; no account and no key.
- **What leaves this computer:** the words you search for (and the contact you give, if any), to
  commons.wikimedia.org and archive.org. Files come from upload.wikimedia.org and the Internet Archive's servers
  (`*.archive.org`).
- **Who starts a run:** anyone, and Claude as a safe step: it is free, uses no key and sends only words.

Wikimedia asks every tool for a way to reach the person using it; give an email or web address as `contact` if you
run it often. Videos from Commons come as WebM (the original or a copy Wikimedia made, at most 1080 lines high);
videos from the Internet Archive as MP4. Files over 500 MB are left out. Old film and photographs search best with
period words: "harbour 1920s", "steam train", "city street 1950".

abilities.name: pexels-stock
abilities.title: Stock videos and photos from Pexels
abilities.does: Finds free stock videos or photos on Pexels that match a few words and brings them in, each with its licence and the photographer's credit.
abilities.notes:
# Stock videos and photos from Pexels

Searches Pexels for a few words and brings in up to six videos (an MP4 up to 1920 wide, the closest to Full HD) or
photos (about 1,900 px wide). Each file keeps its licence, its page on Pexels and the credit line Pexels asks for
("Video by … on Pexels"): a clip records them as its rights, a photo on its source, and a delivery lists them with
its credits.

- **Licence of the files:** the Pexels License — free to use and change, credit not required but asked for. Not
  allowed: selling unchanged copies, showing identifiable people in a bad light, implying they endorse you. Pexels'
  API guidelines ask that you show where the files came from: keep the credit line in the description.
- **Licence of this ability's code:** MIT.
- **Cost:** free. Pexels allows 200 requests an hour and 20,000 a month per key; one run makes one search and one
  request per file.
- **Key:** `pexels`, free with a Pexels account (pexels.com/api). An owner adds it on each computer:
  `metarush ability setup pexels-stock --key pexels`. The code never sees it: MetaRush puts it in the
  Authorization header, only on requests to api.pexels.com.
- **What leaves this computer:** the words you search for, to api.pexels.com. Files come from images.pexels.com and
  videos.pexels.com without the key. A video Pexels offers only from another host is left out.
- **Who starts a run:** a person, each time (it uses a key).

Good searches are short and concrete: "ocean waves at dusk", "city traffic night", "hands typing laptop". Use
`kind: photos` for stills and `orientation: portrait` for shorts.
